overview:
A revolution that began in the far eastern province of Khurasan brought down the Umayyad dynasty in 750 and installed a family descended from the Prophet Muhammad's uncle, al-Abbas, at the head of the Muslim world. The new rulers shifted its centre of gravity eastward from Syria to Iraq, and in 762 al-Mansur laid out a round city on the Tigris — Baghdad — that within a century may have held half a million people. The Abbasid state drew heavily on Persian administrative practice: a vizier and a salaried bureaucracy, provincial governors, a postal and intelligence service. Its early caliphs, above all Harun al-Rashid and his son al-Ma'mun, presided over the period usually called the golden age, when a sustained, well-funded movement translated Greek, Persian, Syriac and Indian works on medicine, astronomy, mathematics and philosophy into Arabic, and when paper spread from the east into everyday administrative and scholarly use. The revolution had promised equality for non-Arab Muslims, and while the reality fell well short of the slogan, Arabic became the shared language of a genuinely cosmopolitan learned culture stretching from Central Asia to the Atlantic.

Political unity was the first thing to go. Al-Andalus never accepted Abbasid rule at all, and by the ninth century North Africa, Egypt and much of Iran were in the hands of dynasties that paid the caliph respect rather than revenue. The murder of al-Mutawakkil by his own Turkish soldiers in 861 opened the "anarchy at Samarra," a decade in which the slave-soldier corps that caliphs had built to free themselves from Arab tribal armies made and unmade rulers instead. In 945 the Buyids, a Shia dynasty from northern Iran, took Baghdad; in 1055 the Seljuk Turks displaced them. For two centuries the caliph was a sanctioning authority rather than a governing one — the man whose name was read in Friday prayers and struck on coins, while others commanded the troops. That was not nothing: the office remained the pivot of Sunni political legitimacy, and it was in these centuries that Islamic law, theology and Sufism took much of their lasting shape. From the 1130s some caliphs, notably al-Nasir, clawed back real territorial power in Iraq and western Iran.

That revival ended abruptly. In 1258 Hulegu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, besieged Baghdad after al-Musta'sim refused his demands; the city fell in February and the caliph was rolled in a carpet and trampled to death, Mongol custom forbidding the spilling of royal blood on the ground. A branch of the family was later maintained in Cairo under Mamluk protection until the Ottoman conquest of 1517, but as a ceremonial fiction rather than a state.
significance: For five centuries the Abbasid caliphate supplied the frame within which a great deal of what we now call Islamic civilisation was built — its legal schools, its theological controversies, its scientific and philosophical vocabulary. The translation movement it funded preserved and extended Greek learning that was then largely unread in Latin Europe, and returned it, through Arabic, to twelfth-century Spain and Sicily and thence to the medieval West; Arabic mathematical and medical texts remained European teaching material for centuries. Just as consequential was the political precedent: after 945 the caliphate demonstrated that religious legitimacy and armed power could be held by different hands, a separation that shaped Sunni political theory long after Baghdad fell. The end of the line in 1258 became, in later memory, the symbolic close of an era — though historians now argue that framing owes more to hindsight than to what actually happened to Baghdad afterwards.
coverage: Written from general reference accounts rather than the Arabic chronicle tradition itself, and the dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date. Two things are genuinely uncertain rather than merely summarised: the casualty figures for 1258, which range from Hulegu's own 200,000 to Muslim sources' two million and which modern scholars treat as inflated — possibly by deaths from a concurrent epidemic — and the long-assumed claim that the sack destroyed Baghdad's libraries and ended the Islamic golden age, which recent work disputes by showing major libraries teaching again within two years. Much of the surviving narrative record for the early caliphate comes from later Abbasid-era historians with reasons to justify the dynasty's rise, and the provinces that broke away are far better documented from their own side than from Baghdad's.
